chunks: ESC vs single-phase motor driver. The question: What is the difference between an ESC and a single-phase motor driver? What additional functionality may an ESC offer?
A simple motor driver (an H-bridge) takes a direction and a speed setting and lets a brushed motor do the rest, because the brushes switch the coils.
The speed setting is a PWM duty: the fraction of time the power is switched on. An ESC for a brushless motor has to do the coil switching itself.
So it needs three pairs of switches, position sensing, and firmware (software built into the chip) that decides what to switch next.
An H-bridge is like a reversing switch on a toy train: forward, reverse, faster, slower. The train does the rest.
An ESC is more like a conductor directing every musician in sequence, listening to the room to know when to cue the next one.
The analogy has one gap: the ESC also includes everything the reversing switch does, such as setting the speed with PWM.
An H-bridge. Q1 and Q4 on drive the motor one way; Q3 and Q2 on drive it the other way; both low-sides on is brake.
Compare with the three-phase bridge in "How BLDC motors work": it has a third leg and nothing like "one motor between two midpoints".
H-bridge: four switches that drive a brushed motor in either direction. Half-bridge: one pair of switches. An ESC has three, one per motor wire.
Commutation: choosing which coils to power as the rotor (the spinning part) turns. Hall sensor: a sensor that tells the controller where the rotor is.
DShot: a digital throttle protocol used by many ESCs.
For a brushed motor, an H-bridge has 4 switches. You tell it "forward, 50% duty" and the motor runs. It needs no idea where the rotor is.
For a brushless motor, an ESC has 3 half-bridges, which is 6 switches .
Every few degrees of rotor movement, it must choose one of six switching states, based on Hall sensors or back-EMF. That choice is the extra intelligence.
That is the whole idea: the ESC is a driver plus commutation.
"A single-phase driver is an H-bridge: it gives a brushed motor a direction and a PWM duty, and the commutator does the smart part mechanically.
An ESC drives three phases with six switches and must do the commutation itself, so it needs rotor position from Hall sensors or back-EMF, and firmware for startup and sequencing.
ESCs also add a throttle protocol, braking and regeneration, current and thermal protection, a BEC, and telemetry."
